title: Jermuk Airport
subtitle: Announced, re-announced, announced again. The valley is still a dead end.
summary: Armenia made the mountain spa town of Jermuk a state-priority tourism centre in 2008 and planned an airport to bring 100,000 international visitors a year straight to its mineral springs. Within a year the deputy minister for urban development called the site a cul-de-sac outside the main air corridor, no funding ever followed, and a 2028 target announced in December 2025 came with no contract and no contractor.
lesson: When a senior official publicly contradicts a policy and nobody resolves it, the project is dead long before anyone cancels it.
locationRole: Proposed airport site above the spa town

title: Anaklia Deepwater Port
subtitle: Georgia's gateway to the Middle Corridor got as far as a dredger and a tribunal.
summary: A consortium of Georgian, American, French, Dutch, Chinese and Korean firms began dredging Georgia's first deepwater container port in December 2017, with $620 million committed to phase one of a $2.5 billion scheme. The government terminated the agreement in January 2020 when the partners could not close a $120 million equity injection and a $400 million loan, and in 2024 an arbitration tribunal upheld the termination with no compensation for the $75 million already spent.
lesson: Financing that is nearly closed is not financing; the remaining gap hands your counterparty a lawful reason to walk away.
locationRole: Port site on the Black Sea coast

title: Auckland Light Rail
subtitle: Seven years and a quarter of a billion dollars, and not one metre of track.
summary: From 2017 Auckland planned a 24 kilometre, partly tunnelled light rail line from the central city to the airport, with estimates climbing from NZ$9.8 billion to as much as NZ$19 billion across successive redesigns. The incoming government cancelled it on 14 January 2024, by which point roughly NZ$228 million had gone on design, consultants and consultation and no track had been laid.
lesson: A scope that grows faster than the funding decision will eventually be cancelled by whoever inherits it.
locationRole: Planned route from the city centre to the airport

title: The Auckland Tramways
subtitle: A hundred and eighteen million rides a year, then the rails were sold for scrap.
summary: Auckland's electric tramway opened in 1902 and grew past 70 kilometres of track, carrying 118 million boardings a year by the 1940s when public transport took more than half of all urban journeys. The last tram ran on 29 December 1956, the rails, wires and poles were removed and scrapped, and public transport's share of trips fell below 10 percent by the 1970s.
lesson: Removing working infrastructure is a decision with a fifty-year tail; the ridership does not return when the policy does.
locationRole: Tram network spine on Queen Street

title: The Khazar Islands
subtitle: Forty-one islands and the world's tallest tower, priced in oil at a hundred dollars.
summary: Developer Ibrahim Ibrahimov began dredging 41 artificial islands across 3,000 hectares of Caspian shallows in November 2010, planning a city for one million people crowned by the 1,050 metre Azerbaijan Tower, at a cost above $100 billion. Oil fell from over $100 to $42 a barrel by March 2015, Ibrahimov was arrested that May over a $57 million state loan he could not service, and the ecology ministry refused approval that October.
lesson: A project underwritten by a single commodity price is a bet on that price, whatever the renderings say.
locationRole: Reclaimed island site in the Caspian

title: Zira Island
subtitle: A carbon-neutral resort drawn on top of the state oil company's gas wells.
summary: Bjarke Ingels Group published a $3 billion masterplan in February 2009 for a carbon-neutral community on a one square kilometre Caspian island, its buildings shaped as the silhouettes of Azerbaijan's seven mountains and powered by its own solar, wind and water systems. The island sat on gas extraction infrastructure controlled by SOCAR, no relocation was ever negotiated, and the scheme was neither built nor formally cancelled.
lesson: Establish who already controls the ground before you design what is meant to stand on it.
locationRole: Island site in Baku Bay

title: The Beirut to Damascus Railway
subtitle: The last train out of Beirut carried eight hundred goats.
summary: The narrow-gauge line from Beirut's Mar Mikhael terminus to Damascus was inaugurated in August 1895 and ran for 81 years across 147 kilometres, with Rayak junction alone employing 2,500 people. The civil war ended it in 1976 and Lebanon's roughly 400 kilometres of track have lain unused since, with UNESCO funding repairs to the terminus building after the 2020 port explosion but no plan to restore service.
lesson: Infrastructure outlives the state that built it only if some institution is still funded to maintain it through the bad years.
locationRole: Coastal terminus and depot

title: The Bisri Dam
subtitle: The land was bought and the owners were paid. The paperwork never arrived.
summary: The World Bank's water project for 1.6 million people in Greater Beirut set three conditions before construction could begin: a finalised ecological compensation plan, agreed operating arrangements, and a contractor mobilised on site. Lebanon had already spent about $197 million expropriating land and compensating 861 owners, but met none of the three by the 4 September 2020 deadline, and the Bank cancelled $244 million of undisbursed funds the next day.
lesson: Conditions in a loan agreement are the project; treating them as paperwork to finish later is how the money leaves.
locationRole: Dam site on the Bisri river

title: Solidere
subtitle: Beirut rebuilt its centre and then could not afford to stand in it.
summary: Established in 1994 to rebuild the war-ruined city centre, Solidere took 1.8 million square metres of downtown Beirut, issued shares to expropriated owners, sold about $2.8 billion of property and restored 265 heritage buildings along a widened Corniche. Roughly 585 other heritage structures were demolished, shops closed within eight years of opening, and by 2019 the rebuilt centre was expensive, exclusive and largely empty.
lesson: Rebuilding the fabric is the easy half; if the people who used the place cannot afford to return, the reconstruction has failed.
locationRole: Rebuilt city centre

title: The Matran Tramway Concession
subtitle: He won a monopoly on Damascus transport and refused to widen the streets.
summary: Yusuf Matran petitioned the Ottoman authorities in 1887 for a horse tramway running from Marjeh Square through Al-Midan, Salihiyeh and Douma, and won an exclusive concession in 1889 on condition that he widen the route to nine metres. His company refused the widening, the concession was revoked in July 1903 without a single rail laid, and a Belgian consortium accepted the same terms and opened the first lines in February 1907.
lesson: The condition you refuse is the price of the franchise, and a competitor who pays it takes the whole market.
locationRole: Planned tramway route from Marjeh Square

title: The Badush Dam
subtitle: The dam built to catch the failure of the most dangerous dam in the world.
summary: Iraq began Badush Dam in 1988 to contain the flood that would follow a collapse of the Mosul Dam upstream, whose soluble gypsum foundation has been seeping for decades. Work stopped in 1991 under Gulf War sanctions at roughly 30 to 40 percent complete, a 2005 ministry estimate put completion at $300 million, and neither Badush nor any alternative has been funded since.
lesson: Protective infrastructure is the first thing cut, because its only benefit appears on the day you were trying to avoid.
locationRole: Unfinished dam site on the Tigris

title: The Jaffa to Jerusalem Railway
subtitle: A motorway beat the Ottoman alignment, and the revival cost more than it earned.
summary: Opened on 26 September 1892, the winding line from the coast to Jerusalem ran for 106 years until Israel Railways closed it on 14 August 1998, by which point Highway 1 had cut service to one train a day in each direction. A partial revival from 2003 cost NIS 540 million against a NIS 330 million plan, and after 2020 Israel Railways declined to restore Jerusalem service at all.
lesson: Once a faster route is built beside an old alignment, reviving the old one costs more than it can ever recover.
locationRole: Coastal terminus at Jaffa

title: Intel Fab 38
subtitle: A cleanroom with the power and cooling installed and no machines going in.
summary: Israel granted Intel $3.2 billion in December 2023, its largest ever subsidy to a private company, toward a $25 billion fabrication plant at Kiryat Gat due to open in 2028. Construction froze by mid-2024 with only the first cleanroom shell finished, the contractor workforce fell from 5,500 to about 2,000, and by July 2025 Intel was discussing closing the existing Fab 28 and its 3,500 jobs as well.
lesson: A subsidy buys a commitment, not a schedule; the grantor ends up carrying the risk of the grantee's own restructuring.
locationRole: Semiconductor fabrication site

title: The Kandahar Diesel Generators
subtitle: A temporary fix that outlived the permanent one it was bridging to.
summary: The United States built two 10 megawatt diesel plants in Kandahar in 2011, about $143.5 million of construction plus $140 million budgeted for fuel, to carry the city until a third turbine at the Kajaki Dam and its transmission lines were finished. Kajaki's Unit 2 never arrived, the Afghan utility could not collect enough revenue to buy fuel, and American subsidies ended in September 2014, leaving the plants effectively defunct by 2015.
lesson: A stopgap is only as sound as the permanent solution it assumes; when that slips you have bought a permanent liability.
locationRole: Diesel power plants serving the city

title: Leonardo's Golden Horn Bridge
subtitle: The sultan's clerks filed the design under the wrong man's name.
summary: Around 1502 Leonardo da Vinci designed a single-arch masonry bridge to span some 240 metres of the Golden Horn at a height of 43 metres, using parabolic abutments that would not be widely adopted for centuries. Ottoman officials recorded the author as a Ricardo of Genoa, no commission followed as the state turned to its Safavid wars, and MIT engineers only confirmed the design would have stood in 2019.
lesson: Attribution is not vanity; a decision-maker who cannot tell whose judgement they are buying will not buy it.
locationRole: Proposed crossing of the Golden Horn

title: Burj Al Babas
subtitle: Five hundred and eighty-seven Gothic castles, roofless, on a Turkish hillside.
summary: A Turkish developer began building 732 identical Gothic chateau villas near Mudurnu in 2014 for Gulf buyers, and had erected about 587 of them by 2018 on roughly $200 million of investment. The lira collapsed that summer, foreign-currency debt of around 20 million pounds became unpayable, Gulf purchasers cancelled, and the company went bankrupt, leaving hollow shells with no roofs, plumbing or wiring.
lesson: Building on schedule proves nothing if your revenue and your debt are denominated in different currencies.
locationRole: Villa development outside Mudurnu

title: Kanal Istanbul
subtitle: A second Bosphorus, opposed by four Istanbullus in five, still officially alive.
summary: Announced in April 2011 as a 45 kilometre artificial waterway from the Black Sea to the Marmara at an estimated $15 billion to $25 billion, the canal got as far as a foundation stone for the Sazlidere Bridge in June 2021 and no further. Turkish courts struck down its zoning and permits, polls put opposition in Istanbul at 77 to 80 percent, no lender would finance it, and the government still calls it delayed rather than cancelled.
lesson: Refusing to cancel a project you cannot fund freezes the land and starves the alternatives for as long as the refusal lasts.
locationRole: Planned canal corridor northwest of the city

title: The Line
subtitle: Nine million people in a mirrored wall. Two point four kilometres of trench.
summary: Unveiled in January 2021, The Line was to be a 170 kilometre linear city 200 metres wide and 500 metres tall, housing nine million people for $500 billion. By September 2025 more than $50 billion had produced 2.4 kilometres of foundation, an internal audit put the true cost to complete at about $8.8 trillion by 2080 and found deliberate manipulation of the finances, and the population target had fallen to 300,000.
lesson: A forecast that is only revised once reality makes it indefensible was never functioning as a control.
locationRole: Foundation works on the Red Sea coast

title: King Abdullah Economic City
subtitle: Two million residents were planned. Ten thousand turned up.
summary: Announced in December 2005 and built by Emaar Properties on $27 billion of investment, King Abdullah Economic City was to be Saudi Arabia's largest free-trade zone and home to two million people by 2035. Two decades on it holds ten to fifteen thousand residents; the port and some industry took hold, but the residential city and the service economy meant to employ it never arrived, and the target date was pushed from 2010 to 2020 to 2035.
lesson: Infrastructure can be built to order; the employers and residents who justify it cannot.
locationRole: New city site north of Jeddah

title: The Bootless Bay Railway
subtitle: Copper, a smelter and a thousand workers. Four years of traffic, then scrap.
summary: New Guinea Copper Mines built a railway from the Laloki and Dubuna workings to a smelter at Bootless Bay between 1918 and 1921 and ran it from 1922 with about 1,000 Papuan and 100 expatriate staff. Mine accidents, refractory ore, debt and falling copper prices closed it in 1926 after the Australian Treasury refused further funds, and the locomotives were sold for scrap, the last shipped to Japan in 1961.
lesson: An integrated chain built around one ore body fails all at once when the geology disappoints, because nothing in it has a second use.
locationRole: Mine railway and smelter site

title: Dubai Lagoon
subtitle: Sold out in four months, cancelled nineteen years later, never built at all.
summary: Schon Properties launched Dubai Lagoon in December 2005, 54 buildings around two artificial lagoons on 5.7 million square feet, and completed pre-sales by March 2006 against a budget of roughly $600 to $810 million. Land disputes, the 2008 crash and four successive contractors left nothing above preliminary foundations; the Land Department seized the project in 2018 and marked it under cancellation in 2024 with at least 111 investors still in dispute.
lesson: Selling a development before you can build it turns your customers into creditors you have no way to repay.
locationRole: Undeveloped site in Dubai Investment Park

title: The Mahe Beach Hotel
subtitle: Shirley Bassey sang here. The army now uses it for room clearing.
summary: Built in 1975 against a Seychelles ban on multi-storey hotels, the 173-room brutalist resort was the country's flagship property, hosting Shirley Bassey and the 1998 Miss World pageant. It closed around 2007 to 2008, was sold and left unguarded, was stripped of tiles, plumbing and fittings by salvagers, and has since served the Seychelles military as an urban combat training site.
lesson: Once a closed building loses its security, other people spend its salvage value and reopening stops being an option.
locationRole: Abandoned resort on the west coast

title: The Perth Freight Link
subtitle: The bulldozers reached the wetland four months before the election did.
summary: Announced in May 2014, the $1.9 billion Roe 8 to 10 scheme was to run 23 kilometres of freight road from Kewdale to Fremantle port, through the Beeliar Wetlands and Noongar heritage sites that the state environmental authority had rejected in January 2013. Construction began in late 2016, the incoming McGowan government suspended it in March 2017 having campaigned against it, and it was formally struck from the pipeline in January 2025.
lesson: Starting construction to make a project irreversible does not work when the objection is political rather than financial.
locationRole: Roe Highway alignment through the wetlands

title: The Red Sea to Dead Sea Conveyance
subtitle: Two seas, four hundred metres of fall, and nobody willing to pay.
summary: A trilateral agreement signed in May 2005 by Israel, Jordan and the Palestinian Authority proposed a $10 billion pipeline from Aqaba to the Lisan basin with desalination and hydropower, using the 400 metre drop to slow a Dead Sea falling about a metre a year. Israel never committed its expected share of more than $1 billion, the effects of brine discharge were never resolved, and Jordan abandoned the scheme in June 2021 in favour of desalination alone.
lesson: A shared problem does not produce shared funding; an agreement with three signatures and no paying party is a study.
locationRole: Planned intake on the Red Sea

title: Mineral Beach
subtitle: The car park went overnight. Then the spa, then the whole shoreline.
summary: Mineral Beach at Mitzpe Shalem drew about 250,000 visitors a year until June 2015, when a sinkhole opened overnight and swallowed its car park and bath buildings; Ein Gedi Beach closed the following year for the same reason. Roughly 5,000 sinkholes have formed since the 1980s as the falling sea lets groundwater dissolve buried salt, and the abandoned facilities are now toured as a disaster site.
lesson: When the hazard is a trend rather than an event, no repair restores the site, because the ground keeps moving underneath it.
locationRole: Closed spa and bathing beach

title: Madinat Al-Hareer
subtitle: Kuwait reorganised the agency in charge four times and never broke ground.
summary: Announced in 2004 and endorsed by Kuwait's Council of Ministers in November 2007, Silk City was a 250 square kilometre development for 700,000 people costing $100 to $132 billion, crowned by the 1,001 metre Burj Mubarak Al Kabir. Responsibility passed from the municipality to the investment authority and planning council, then to a new land authority in 2012, then into the Northern Economic Zone, and construction never started.
lesson: Restructuring the responsible body is how an organisation avoids deciding; each reorganisation buys years and delivers nothing.
locationRole: Planned city site on Kuwait Bay

title: Shahestan Pahlavi
subtitle: A ceremonial capital cut into seven islands by four expressways.
summary: Llewelyn-Davies International's 1974 masterplan for 554 hectares of north-central Tehran laid out ministries, a national library, a 12 hectare plaza and a 30 metre monument at an estimated $3 billion, drawing competition entries from Kenzo Tange and Louis Kahn before earthworks began in 1975. The 1979 revolution repudiated it, and six competing plans plus four expressways built between 1998 and 2005 left the site as fragments separated by asphalt.
lesson: A site can be fully built out and still fail, if every successor plan is drawn without reference to the last.
locationRole: Planned civic centre on the Abbasabad hills

title: Pardis City
subtitle: Towers finished, roads to nowhere, and no cars in the satellite photographs.
summary: Under the Mehr housing scheme Iran contracted Turkey's Kuzu Group from 2001 to build a satellite city of about 37,000 units fifty kilometres east of Tehran, complete with hospitals, schools and transport. The first three phases filled with roughly 74,000 residents facing faulty sewage, weak power and commutes of two to three hours, and inflation plus the 2018 return of sanctions drove Kuzu out, leaving about 11,000 unfinished units and empty finished blocks.
lesson: Housing without transport and utilities is not housing; the missing connections decide whether anyone can actually live there.
locationRole: Satellite city site below Mount Damavand
